questions.lead: A calendar year is drawn at random from 1950 to 2022. We won't say which.
questions.ask: The S&P 500 rose 20% or more over the year.
questions.claim: A calendar year is drawn at random from 1950 to 2022. We won't say which. The S&P 500 rose 20% or more over the year.
questions.fact: It was 1954: the S&P 500 rose 40.8% from the December 1953 average to the December 1954 average (price only; dividends are not counted). Across the other 72 years from 1950 to 2022, it rose 20% or more in 24%.
questions.why: Stocks rise in most years, but a typical year swings a long way either way. A rising market is the base rate, not a promise, and a fall of 10% or more is not a freak event.
questions.src_name: Robert Shiller's long-run U.S. stock data (S&P 500 monthly average price, CPI), via the open datasets project

questions.lead: A year is drawn at random from those that came right after a falling year (1951 to 2022).
questions.ask: The S&P 500 rose that year.
questions.claim: A year is drawn at random from those that came right after a falling year (1951 to 2022). The S&P 500 rose that year.
questions.fact: It was 2019, after a fall of 3.6% in 2018: the S&P 500 rose 23.7% from the December 2018 average to the December 2019 average (price only; dividends are not counted). Of the other 19 years that came right after a falling year, it rose in 79%.
questions.why: One year tells you little about the next. After a bad year or a great one the market has still gone up more often than down, so 'it is due for a fall' or 'it has to bounce' are stories, not forecasts.
questions.src_name: Robert Shiller's long-run U.S. stock data (S&P 500 monthly average price, CPI), via the open datasets project

questions.lead: A 5-year stretch is drawn at random, starting in a year from 1950 to 2017. We won't say which.
questions.ask: The S&P 500 ended the stretch lower than it began.
questions.claim: A 5-year stretch is drawn at random, starting in a year from 1950 to 2017. We won't say which. The S&P 500 ended the stretch lower than it began.
questions.fact: It was 2007 to 2012: the S&P 500 fell 4% from the December 2007 average to the December 2012 average (price only; dividends are not counted). Across the other 67 stretches of 5 years from 1950 on, it ended higher in 81%. Neighbouring stretches overlap, so there are fewer independent cases than that.

questions.claim: Look at the US stock market as a whole since 1926 and ask where its gains over Treasury bills came from. It took more than 50% of all listed stocks to account for the market's entire net gain.
questions.fact: In Hendrik Bessembinder's study, the entire gain of the US stock market since 1926 is attributable to the best-performing 4% of listed stocks.
questions.why: A handful of giant winners produce the market's returns. Own only a few stocks and you will probably miss them, while a broad index owns them all.

questions.claim: A drug candidate is in its Phase II trial, the first real test of whether it works. Fewer than 20% of candidates like it move on to Phase III.
questions.fact: BIO's data for 2011 to 2020 (4,933 programmes): 28.9% of candidates moved from Phase II to Phase III, the lowest rate of the four stages.
questions.why: Phase II is where most drug hopes end: showing that a drug works is much harder than showing it is safe. Early promise is cheap; evidence of effect is not.

questions.fact: Industry data on 12,728 drug programmes (BIO, Informa and QLS, 2011 to 2020): 7.9% of the programmes that entered Phase I were eventually approved.
questions.why: The drug pipeline is a funnel with a narrow end: most candidates fail somewhere along the way, however good the early news. A promising first trial is a weak signal of an eventual medicine.
